scenes.name: Rapcore y New Metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Body Count, el grupo del rapero Ice-T, abre el rapcore con temas atractivos para chicos de todas las razas; a finales de la década las voces rapeadas se ponen de moda, aunque pocos de esos grupos son metal. Spin dedica en agosto de 1998 un reportaje al «New Metal» (Korn, Limp Bizkit con su DJ fijo), un híbrido que bebe tanto del rock alternativo, el hip-hop y el hardcore del skate californiano como de Black Sabbath y Slayer, y Rolling Stone lleva en febrero de 1999 a Rob Zombie en portada con los «10 mejores grupos de metal». Weinstein se pregunta por qué se llama metal a lo que sus músicos no quieren que se llame así: la etiqueta da una imagen más blanca y más rock, y su uso promiscuo es a la vez prueba y causa del regreso del metal. ¿Es metal Rage Against the Machine? ¿Y Sevendust o Limp Bizkit?

podcast.title: `Cafe Flesh` Sample (1982)
podcast.body: The distinct moaning in Rob Zombie and White Zombie's song "More Human Than Human" is sampled from the 1982 sci-fi movie `Cafe Flesh`, which depicts a post-nuclear world where most surviving humans become ill if they attempt sex, leading to live sex shows for their benefit. "The sample is taken from a 1982 sci-fi movie called Cafe Flesh. After the world is nearly annihilated in a nuclear war, they're surviving humans find that they get sick when they try to have sex. The moaning comes from someone participating in a live sex show conducted for the benefit of those humans who can't have sex anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dreadlocks in 1990s Rock and Metal
podcast.body: Rob Zombie was among the musicians in the 1990s who sported dreadlocks, contributing to the hairstyle's increasing prevalence across rock and metal genres. "And then through the 90s, dreads appeared on everyone from Rob Zombie and Zach from Raging Us the Machine to Jonathan Davis of Corn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Use of Marshall Amplifiers
podcast.body: Rob Zombie is listed among hundreds of musicians, both famous and lesser-known, who utilize Jim Marshall's amplifiers. This inclusion underscores the enduring popularity and critical role Marshall amplifiers play in achieving loud, powerful rock sounds across many decades. "Over the decades, Jim's amplifiers became synonymous with loud, powerful rock and today they used by slash, oasis, the death tones, rob zombie, Paul Weller, some 41, pop erosion, hundreds of others, famous and not so famous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Horror Film Directing
podcast.body: Beyond music, Rob Zombie has directed movies that feature graphic content, including torture, skinning people alive, and necrophilia. "We should take the movies he's directed into account because a lot of torture and skinny people alive, necrophilia, stuff like that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Porn and B-Grade Movie Samples
podcast.body: Rob Zombie's heavy music often incorporates samples from porn films and B-grade movies to enhance its horror aesthetic. "all his horror, heavy music, with samples from porn films and B-grade movies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Production Assistant on Pee-wee's Playhouse (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: Before becoming known as a movie director and horror metal artist, Rob Zombie worked as a production assistant on the television show "Pee-wee's Playhouse" in the mid-1980s. Additionally, he was employed by a company responsible for producing commercials for Twizzlers. "movie director and horror metal guy Rob Zombie, was once a production assistant on Peewee's Playhouse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tour Bus Movie Habits
podcast.body: Rob Zombie mentions that while on tour, he tries to stock up on movies he hasn't seen. However, inevitably, one "ridiculous" movie, such as *Austin Powers* or *Dumb and Dumber*, becomes a communal favorite and is watched "a thousand times" by everyone on the bus, leading to repetitive quotes and inside jokes throughout the tour. "It'll be something like Austin Powers. There's always some movie that pops up that once it was dumb and dumber, that was the movie that everyone watched like a thousand times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Proposed Concert Rating Systems – Would Bar Minors from Manson, Zombie, and Korn Shows
xref.body: Proposed legislation in Michigan and New Jersey sought to implement concert rating systems that would prohibit people under 18 from attending concerts by artists including Marilyn Manson, Rob Zombie, and Korn, with fines and jail terms for promoters who allowed underage admission. "Would prohibit entry to minors at concerts by Marilyn Manson, Rob Zombie, or Korn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shared Influences
xref.body: The two members, TheOGM and Yeti999, met by attending basement punk shows and shared a common appreciation for hardcore music, hip-hop, and horror movies, particularly those directed by Rob Zombie, which inspired their band's formation. "They met going to basement punk shows. They both loved hardcore and they loved hip-hop. They both loved horror movies, especially those directed by Rob Zombie, so why not form a band?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
